heading: accept()
content: Accepts a pending connection on a socket. Returns a new socket object usable to send and receive data on the connection, and the address bound to the socket on the other end. The newly created socket is non-inheritable. The socket must be bound to an address and listening for connections. The return value is a pair (conn, address) where conn is a new socket object usable to send and receive data on the connection.

heading: bind(address)
content: Bind the socket to address. The socket must not already be bound. The format of address depends on the address family. For AF_INET the address is a tuple (host, port). For AF_INET6 the address is a four-tuple (host, port, flowinfo, scope_id). For AF_UNIX the address is a string representing a filesystem path. If the socket is already bound, an OSError is raised indicating the address is already in use.

heading: close()
content: Mark the socket closed. The underlying system resource (the file descriptor) is freed. All future operations on the socket object will fail with an OSError. The remote end will receive no more data after the socket is closed. Sockets are automatically closed when they are garbage-collected, but it is recommended to close them explicitly using a with statement or calling close directly to ensure timely release of resources.

heading: connect(address)
content: Connect to a remote socket at address. The format of address depends on the address family. If the connection is interrupted by a signal, the method waits until the connection completes, or raises a timeout exception on timeout. If the connection fails, an error is raised. For non-blocking sockets, the method raises BlockingIOError when the connection cannot be completed immediately, and select can be used to wait for completion.

heading: getpeername()
content: Return the remote address to which the socket is connected. This is useful to find the port number of a remote IPv4/v6 socket, for instance. The format of the returned address depends on the address family. On some systems this function is not supported. If the socket has not been connected, an error is raised. For connected sockets the address information includes the remote host and port.

heading: getsockname()
content: Return the socket own address. This is useful to find the port number of an IPv4/v6 socket, for instance. The return value is a tuple containing the host and port for AF_INET sockets. For AF_INET6 sockets it returns a four-tuple. This is particularly useful when the socket was bound to port 0, which tells the operating system to pick an available port automatically.

heading: listen(backlog)
content: Enable a server to accept connections. The backlog parameter specifies the number of unaccepted connections that the system will allow before refusing new connections. If not specified, a default reasonable value is chosen. A backlog of at least 0 is required. Many systems silently limit the backlog to 5. On Linux the default is 128. Once the backlog limit is reached, new connection attempts are refused.

heading: recv(bufsize)
content: Receive data from the socket. The return value is a bytes object representing the data received. The maximum amount of data to be received at once is specified by bufsize. A returned empty bytes object indicates that the client has disconnected. For non-blocking sockets, a BlockingIOError is raised if no data is available. The optional flags argument defaults to 0 and has the same meaning as for the Unix recv system call.

heading: send(data)
content: Send data to the socket. The socket must be connected to a remote socket. Returns the number of bytes sent. Applications are responsible for checking that all data has been sent; if only some of the data was transmitted, the application needs to attempt delivery of the remaining data. The optional flags argument has the same meaning as for recv. Unlike sendall, this method does not guarantee complete delivery.

heading: setsockopt(level, optname, value)
content: Set the value of the given socket option. The needed symbolic constants are defined in the socket module SO_REUSEADDR, SO_KEEPALIVE, etc. The value argument can be an integer, None, or a bytes-like object representing a buffer. In the later case it is up to the caller to ensure that the bytestring contains the proper bits. Most socket options apply at the SOL_SOCKET level for cross-platform compatibility.

heading: shutdown(how)
content: Shut down one or both halves of the connection. If how is SHUT_RD, further receives are disallowed. If how is SHUT_WR, further sends are disallowed. If how is SHUT_RDWR, further sends and receives are disallowed. Depending on the platform, shutting down one half of the connection can also close the opposite half. Unlike close, shutdown does not release the underlying resource immediately.
